catalog_quote: [p. 12, §1 Akzent] Der Akzent ist grundsätzlich der gleiche wie im Neupersischen. Auch andere Mundarten und nicht zuletzt das Neupersische schwanken in ihrer Betonung, insofern innerhalb eines Satzganzen die Endbetonung der Einzelwörter oft aufgehoben erscheint (Sandhi-Wirkung). [p. 13] Der Akzent erscheint im Satz nicht immer an der Stelle, wo man ihn erwartet; so auch in np. yekí statt yéki, digarí statt digári usw. Im Chunsari tritt die Anfangsbetonung des den Satz beginnenden Wortes stark hervor; d.h. die erste Silbe des Satzes (außer vä, o „und”) erhält sehr oft einen kräftigen Akzent, der den Endakzent des Wortes überklingt: ... new_statements.quote: [p.12] Der Akzent ist grundsätzlich der gleiche wie im Neupersischen. Auch andere Mundarten und nicht zuletzt das Neupersische schwanken in ihrer Betonung, insofern innerhalb eines Satzganzen die Endbetonung der Einzelwörter oft aufgehoben erscheint (Sandhi-Wirkung). [p.13] ... Im Chunsari tritt die Anfangsbetonung des den Satz beginnenden Wortes stark hervor; d.h. die erste Silbe des Satzes (außer vä, o „und”) erhält sehr oft einen kräftigen Akzent, der den Endakzent des Wortes überklingt ... Am Satzende liegt die andere große Tonstelle. [p.341] Der Akzent wird nur dort bezeichnet, wo er nicht auf der letzten Silbe liegt. [p.48] Der Plural wird durch Anhängen von betontem -ā (np. -hā) gebildet.
new_statements.translation: [p.12] The accent is fundamentally the same as in New Persian. Other dialects too, and not least New Persian, fluctuate in their stressing, in that within a sentence-whole the final stress of the individual words often appears suspended (sandhi effect). [p.13] ... In Chunsari the initial stressing of the word that begins the sentence stands out strongly; i.e. the first syllable of the sentence (except vä, o 'and') very often receives a strong accent which drowns out the word's final accent ... At the end of the sentence lies the other major stress position. [p.341] The accent is marked only where it does not lie on the last syllable. [p.48] The plural is formed by adding stressed -ā (NP -hā).
new_statements.citation: Eilers, Wilhelm & Ulrich Schapka. 1976. Westiranische Mundarten aus der Sammlung Wilhelm Eilers, Bd. 1: Die Mundart von Chunsar. Wiesbaden: Franz Steiner.

I rendered the page images and read them directly: PDF p.36 = book p.12 carries 'LAUTLEHRE.. section 1 Akzent: Der Akzent ist grundsaetzlich der gleiche wie im Neupersischen. Auch andere Mundarten und nicht zuletzt das Neupersische schwanken in ihrer Betonung, insofern innerhalb eines Satzganzen die Endbetonung der Einzelwoerter oft aufgehoben erscheint (Sandhi-Wirkung)' with fn.2 'Es ist ein Fehler vieler Mundartpublikationen, dass sie den Akzent nicht oder nur ungenuegend aufzeichnen'; PDF p.37 = book p.13: 'Der Akzent erscheint im Satz nicht immer an der Stelle, wo man ihn erwartet; so auch in np. yekí statt yéki, diga…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent as in New Persian: on the final syllable of the word (nominal inflections such as plural -ā take the stress); non-final accent is the marked case (Persian-type exceptions, e.g. certain clitics/particles and verbal prefixes, are implied by 'as in New Persian' but not itemised). In connected speech word-final stress is frequently overridden: the sentence-initial syllable often carries a strong accent and the sentence end is the other main prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Eilers states (p. 11 fn. 1) that he could not record finer distinctions such as main vs secondary stress (Haupt- und Nebenton) or dynamic vs pitch accent; no secondary-stress rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent 'as in New Persian' implies the Persian non-final cases; Eilers notes NP-style fluctuation (yekí ~ yéki, digarí ~ dígari); sentence-initial words take initial stress overriding Endakzent (except the conjunctions vä, o 'and'); Endbetonung often suspended sentence-internally (sandhi); glossary marks only non-final accents. Mann & Hadank 1926 add that the determinative suffix -ä is fully stressed while accusative -ä is at most half-stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level default is final (citation/lexical form, per glossary convention); Eilers explicitly separates this from sentence accent, where initial and final positions of the sentence attract prominence and word-final stress may be neutralised. Data: dictated narrative texts from one Khunsar-born informant (1940-41) plus 1974 field notes.
new_statements.identity_note: Eilers & Schapka 1976 describe the dialect of the town of Khunsar (Chunsar/Khvansar) as dictated by one native informant (Mehbud) in 1940-41, with Eilers' own 1974 notes from the Khunsar valley and neighbouring Vanešan (Vaneshani, treated as a close sister dialect; Glottolog files it with khun1255's western CPD neighbours). This is the same variety as Glottolog khun1255 / ISO kfm. Mann & Hadank 1926 'Khunsari' is likewise Khunsar town (Mann's 1903 texts).

[p. 13] Im Chunsari tritt die Anfangsbetonung des den Satz beginnenden Wortes stark hervor; d.h. die erste Silbe des Satzes (außer vä, o „und”) erhält sehr oft einen kräftigen Akzent, der den Endakzent des Wortes überklingt [...] Am Satzende liegt die andere große Tonstelle [...] [p. 341] Der Akzent wird nur dort bezeichnet, wo er nicht auf der letzten Silbe liegt.
new_statements.translation: [p. 12] § 1 Accent. The accent is fundamentally the same as in New Persian. Other dialects too, and not least New Persian, waver in their stress, in that within a sentence as a whole the final stress of the individual words often appears suspended (sandhi effect). [p. 13] In Chunsari the initial stress of the word that begins the sentence stands out strongly; i.e. the first syllable of the sentence (except vä, o 'and') very often receives a strong accent which overrides the word's final accent [...] At the end of the sentence lies the other major place of prominence [...] [p. 341] The accent is marked only where it does not fall on the last syllable.

Adds: glossary convention 'accent marked only where non-final' (p. 341) which makes final the default across the lexicon; explicit sentence-level overrides (sentence-initial strong accent, sentence-final prominence, sandhi loss of word-final stress); no primary/secondary or dynamic/pitch distinction recorded (fn. p. 11); stressed plural -á and deictic -á; prefix-stressed verb forms (p. 84). The listed open_url is NOT the grammar but D. N. MacKenzie's one-page review of it (BSOAS 40, 1977), which contains no placement statement, only the remark that the texts are fully accented but no a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the final syllable, as in New Persian (the glossary marks stress only where it is non-final, so final is the default). This is overlaid by sentence-level effects: the first syllable of a sentence (except the conjunction vä/o 'and') very often takes a strong accent that overrides the word's final stress (yág ǧúri tár teräz-u, déštōunā..), sentence-final position is the other major prominence (yäg_tendīrī vs tendíri, nägenendé vs nägenende), and sentence-internal words often lose their final stress (sandhi). The authors admit that accent shifts constantly within the sentence and varies by speaker and tempo (Introduction p. 3; Texts introduction p. 11).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not distinguished. Fn. 1 p. 11 (Texte, Umschrift): 'So unerläßlich mir die Angabe des Akzents erscheint, so wenig habe ich bei der Geschwindigkeit der Niederschrift feinere Unterschiede wie etwa Haupt- und Nebenton angeben können, nicht zu reden von der Differenzierung in Druck- und Tonakzent, die meist kombiniert begegnen.' Acute marks stressed short vowel, a second mark stressed long vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-final stresses are individually marked in the glossary (p. 341). Morphological: plural suffix -á is stressed ('Der Plural wird durch Anhängen von betontem -á (np. -hä) gebildet', Pluralbildung § 1, book p. ~48, scanned) and the anaphoric-deictic suffix -á is 'stets betont' (§ 55 Die Deixis, scanned); verb forms in the paradigms on p. 84 carry stress on the negative/preverb prefix (ná-resäān 'I have not arrived', bá-resä-ye 'you have arrived', hắ kissä-ye), the New Persian-type pattern; p. 84 also notes that in colloquial New Persian accent can distinguish preterite góftam from perfect goftám. p. 26: 'Durch Akzent bedingt direkt bönän „ich sehe” < bävinän' (vowel contraction conditioned by accent). MacKenzie's review (BSOAS 40, 1977, col. 1) says: 'A point is made of the complete accentuation of the texts, but no detailed analysis of word or sentence stress patterns is offered.'
new_statements.identity_note: Eilers' material is the dialect of the town of Khunsar (Chunsar), recorded 1940-41 from a single informant (Mehbud) and revised in the field in 1974 (MacKenzie: 'they all stem from one informant'); fn. 1 p. 12 notes that the umlauted vowels in brackets were recorded in Vānišān in 1974. No other variety is described.
